PostgreSQL 17.10 · patched distribution · fuzzing campaign

A soak run against PostgreSQL 17.10

Twenty-three fuzz targets, two sanitizer builds, run continuously and stopped on a schedule at 08:00 on 27 August 2026. This is what ran, what it covered, and what was changed to make it run.

What this is

Fuzzing means feeding a program millions of generated inputs and watching for it to crash or misbehave. You keep the inputs that reach code nothing has reached before; over time that collection — the corpus — grows into a set of inputs that exercises the program broadly.

This report covers one continuous run against PostgreSQL 17.10 as shipped in the patched distribution, with third-party extensions loaded. It reports the machinery and the measurements. Defect detail is deliberately kept to counts and categories.

23fuzz targets
2sanitizer builds
46target × build cells
2,344,269corpus inputs kept
43.9%of the server executed
782ratchet floors held
8source changes listed

Every one of the 23 targets was fuzzing when the run was stopped. That is worth stating plainly because it was not true at the start of the week: several targets were replaying their saved inputs and never generating new ones, which produces confident-looking logs and no testing at all. Finding and fixing that is a large part of what this campaign did.

How fuzzing works here

A fuzz target is a small program that takes a chunk of bytes and feeds it into one part of PostgreSQL. The fuzzer generates bytes, runs the target, and watches which lines of code get executed.

An input that reaches new code is kept; one that does not is thrown away. The kept inputs are the corpus. Starting a run means replaying the whole corpus first, which costs time but establishes the baseline; only after that does the fuzzer start mutating — making small random changes to look for new behaviour.

A sanitizer is a compiler setting that makes the program check itself as it runs. ASan (address) catches reads and writes outside valid memory. UBSan (undefined behaviour) catches operations the C language does not define, such as signed overflow. The same target is built twice, once under each, because they detect different things.

Two builds were fuzzed — one ASan, one UBSan — giving 46 target × build cells. A third build, compiled for coverage measurement rather than bug detection, is used only to answer “which code did the corpus actually reach?”

The run

The run was stopped on a timer at 2026-08-27 08:00:10 local time, on request, rather than at a natural end. Nothing was mid-write; the stop is a clean shutdown that lets each target finish its current slice.

The run used soak mode: targets are kept continuously busy from a shared pool rather than run in fixed rounds. Rounds restart every target on a schedule, and each restart pays the replay cost again — with a corpus of this size that was consuming most of the machine's time. Soak pays replay once.

RunsSlicesHoursPeriod
Most recent run184310.52026-08-28 20:44 → 2026-08-29 07:12
Whole campaign81,495822026-08-24 19:20 → 2026-08-29 07:12
Runs are detected from the slices themselves — nothing records where one campaign ends and the next begins, but a slice lasts at least 900s, so an hour in which none STARTED means nothing was running. The hours column sums those run spans and therefore excludes the gaps between them: first slice to last is 108 hours, against 82 of actual running. Processor time actually spent fuzzing is the stricter measure again and is not stated — the per-slice budget was not recorded before 2026-08-30 (0 of 1,495 rows carry it so far).
748 core-hours is how much machine the campaign was given: 1,495 slices x 1800s x 1 worker(s), every observed slice log agreeing on both. The multiplication is exact; what is estimated is only that these rows carried no budget of their own, and the figure is offered because every slice log still on disk agrees on the cost. Had they disagreed, nothing would appear here rather than an average over a mixed population.
That is machine ALLOCATED, not processor time burned, and the two diverge enormously by target. Measured this session: spi_query ran at 94–100% of a core while simple_query sat at 2–7%, waiting on the backend rather than computing. Consumption is sampled nowhere, and the containers are --rm, so their cgroup counters go with them.

One entry per fuzz target. Corpus is how many inputs that target has kept. Execs is how many inputs it ran in its final slice. Coverage

Coverage is the share of the program's lines that the corpus actually executes. It answers a question the corpus size cannot: are these inputs reaching the code we care about, or piling up in one corner?

It is measured after the run by replaying the finished corpus against a build compiled to record which lines execute. Each target is measured on its own, one at a time.

Compare the “lines covered” column, not the percentage. Every target links a different set of source files, so each has its own denominator: most sit near 550,000 lines of server code, but a target linking only the client library has a base of about 16,000. A percentage tracks one target over time; across targets it compares two different questions and will rank them wrongly.

All 23 together

Per-target numbers cannot be added up: every target executes the server's startup, its allocator, its error paths, so summing would count those lines twenty-three times. This is the union, computed by merging the raw profile data and counting each line once no matter how many targets reached it.

43.88%of all lines
49.1%of functions
29.8%of branches
772of 1451 files entered
49.5%of lines in those files

The whole is considerably more than its largest part. The single deepest target reaches about 35% on its own; all twenty-three together reach 43.9%. The other twenty-two therefore add roughly 66,677 lines the deepest one never touches, which is the case for keeping the narrow single-purpose harnesses rather than only the broad ones.

Functions reached (49%) sit well above branches taken (30%). That gap is the shape of the remaining work: the campaign gets into about half the functions but takes only about a third of the decisions inside them. What is left is mostly error handling and edge conditions, not unexplored subsystems.

Coverage is measured for all 23 targets, one at a time. Each measurement replays that target's whole corpus against a build compiled to record which lines execute.

“core files the patch touches” is every line of the 265 files the patch series modifies, not the patch itself. The patch adds 26,073 lines into a 114,450-line universe — 22.8% — so the other three quarters is stock PostgreSQL that happens to share a file with a hunk, and the patch’s own lines could be wholly covered or wholly missed without moving this figure much. It also sits above plain core partly because the patch touches tcop, the executor and the parser, which a query fuzzer exercises heavily whether or not they were patched.

What it turned up

Two different numbers get called “findings”, and confusing them overstates the result by more than tenfold.

An artifact is one saved input that made the target crash, run out of memory, or hang. The fuzzer writes one file every time it happens, so a single underlying defect hit repeatedly produces hundreds of them.

A finding is a distinct defect after triage — after those artifacts have been reduced, grouped by signature, and confirmed. That is the number that means something.

Which fuzzer found them

A finding is attributed to a target when the write-up says so outright, or when it names exactly one. A write-up naming several is left unattributed on purpose: those are systemic — a deadline that never fires, a budget eaten by replay — and hit many targets at once. Pinning one on whichever fuzzer is mentioned first would invent a precision the evidence does not have.

Counts only, deliberately. Which component carries which defect, and whether it is reported upstream, is the maintainers’ call to make and not this report’s to pre-empt. The per-target table above shows raw artifact counts so the shape of the run is visible; the artifacts and reproducers are not published here.

The per-target artifact counts are worth reading as a map of where the run spent its luck, not as a scoreboard. Two targets account for most of the raw total, and in both cases that is one signature hit over and over rather than many separate problems.

Every component, and its hash

The fingerprint is eight characters. It answers "are these two runs the same" and nothing else — when it changes it does not say what changed, and two years from now it is not a build recipe. This is the expansion: every input, layer by layer, with the hash that identifies it.

A dot marks something recorded but deliberately not hashed into the fingerprint — the driver script, the build recipe. They shape the build without defining the experiment, and marking them keeps the difference visible instead of implied.

What the gates did not fail on

A ratchet earns its keep by not crying wolf, and every rule that stops it crying wolf also hides something. A report that shows only what passed inherits that blindness, so this section lists what was let through and why.

Three ways it happens. An acknowledgement suppresses a target outright — a decision made deliberately in a commit, but one nobody revisits becomes a finding nobody looked at. The tolerance is "at least a tenth of the record", not "within a tenth of it", so a target can fall by eighty per cent and still pass. And a floor earned under a different configuration is skipped as not comparable, which is correct and still leaves that target unguarded.

protocol, simple_query

The ratchet

A ratchet records the best each target has ever done and fails the run if it later does meaningfully worse. It exists because the dangerous failure in fuzzing is silent: a target that stops working still produces logs, still writes files, and still looks healthy. Only comparison against its own past catches it.

An exec floor is the number of inputs a target has run before. A rate floor is how fast it ran them. Rate matters separately — a target given twice the time can clear its exec floor while running at half speed, and the ratchet should notice.

34workspaces covered

Source changes

Four different kinds of source change are in play, and the difference matters. A patch series is code we were given and are testing. A cherry-pick is an upstream fix pulled back. A patched extension is a local change to third-party code so it survives being fuzzed. Harness code is ours — the fuzz targets themselves.

Only a patched extension could be mistaken for “we found a bug in someone else's software”, and at least one of them is not that: it is a compatibility change so the extension tolerates being driven far harder than it was designed for.

The extension change guards against a lock the extension could take twice against itself under the harness’s call pattern. It is a harness-compatibility fix, not a defect report against that project.

Limits & open items

Stated plainly, because a report that only lists what worked is not much use:

  • Coverage is reproducible to within measurement noise. Every target was measured twice — once one-at-a-time, once with all 23 running concurrently in isolated containers. Twenty of 23 agreed exactly; the other three differed by 3, 4 and 34 lines out of tens of thousands. Two repeats of the same serial method differ by a similar amount, so that is the noise floor of the measurement, not a defect in it.
  • Coverage is a post-hoc snapshot. It was measured after the run against the final corpus, not tracked continuously, so it shows where the corpus ended up rather than how it got there.
  • The coverage build had drifted — now checked automatically. It was built two days before the fuzzing builds and, because its configuration named the unpatched version of one extension, a clean rebuild still produced different software. Coverage from it would have sat beside corpus figures describing a different program. A check now compares the source commit, every shared extension’s version, and the applied patches across all three builds, and refuses to let them diverge silently.
  • Ten of the throughput floors were measured in the wrong unit. A target runs several jobs at once. The execution counts were added together across those jobs, correctly, but so were their durations — and concurrent durations do not add. The resulting speed figure was per-job while the count beside it was the total, and comparing them implied up to 88 hours of work for a two-hour slice. Fixed, and the affected floors were discarded rather than kept: a floor nothing can fail is worse than no floor. The execution-count floors are unaffected.
  • Per-target logs are per-slice. Soak overwrites each target’s log every slice, so the shipped logs hold the final slice, not the whole run. Cumulative history lives in the ratchet series, which is included.
  • Two targets needed restarting during the run. Both drive a real server process and can wedge it; a watchdog restarts them. The underlying cause is understood for one path and not fully for the other.
  • An earlier corpus cap archived a large number of inputs on a diagnosis that turned out to be wrong. They were archived rather than deleted and the counts are shown per target above.
